Reconciliation means restoring a relationship or a state of harmony that was broken. It is the act — or the result — of bringing two things (people, groups, ideas, or records) back into agreement or peaceful coexistence after they have been in conflict, opposition, or disagreement.

Think of it this way: imagine a bridge between two sides. Something happened — a fight, a betrayal, a war, a long silence — and that bridge collapsed. Reconciliation is the process of rebuilding that bridge.

The word almost always implies three things:

  1. There was harmony or agreement before.
  2. Something happened that broke it.
  3. Now, there is a deliberate effort to restore it.
The Different Contexts Where "Reconciliation" is Used

The word is used in several different areas of life. Each is a variation of the same core idea — restoring harmony — applied to a different setting.

1. Between People (Personal/Social)

This is the most common and relatable use. When two people — friends, family members, partners, colleagues — have had a serious conflict or falling out and then work to mend their relationship, that process is called reconciliation.

It is not just about saying "sorry" or "I forgive you." Reconciliation usually involves:

  • Acknowledging what went wrong
  • Understanding each other's perspective
  • Working toward rebuilding trust

Example: After years of not speaking following a bitter argument, the two brothers eventually achieved reconciliation. They didn't forget what happened, but they chose to move forward together.

A crucial nuance: reconciliation does not require pretending nothing happened. It means choosing a future together despite what happened in the past.

2. Between Groups, Communities, or Nations (Political/Historical)

On a larger scale, reconciliation refers to the process by which communities, ethnic groups, or nations that have harmed each other — through war, oppression, injustice, or conflict — work toward mutual understanding and peaceful coexistence.

This kind of reconciliation is often a long, structured, and formal process. It might involve:

  • Official apologies from governments
  • Truth commissions (where past crimes are openly acknowledged and recorded)
  • Reparations (compensation to those who were harmed)
  • Public rituals of healing

Example: After apartheid ended in South Africa, the country established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to help the nation confront its painful history and begin healing. This is one of the most famous examples of national reconciliation in the modern world.

The key idea here: reconciliation does not erase the past. It acknowledges it honestly so that people can live together without ongoing cycles of hatred and revenge.

3. In Religion and Spirituality

In many religious traditions, especially Christianity, reconciliation refers to the restoration of a relationship between humans and God — a relationship seen as broken by sin, wrongdoing, or separation.

Example: The sacrament of reconciliation in the Catholic Church (also called Confession) is the formal practice by which a person confesses their sins and receives forgiveness, restoring their relationship with God.

More broadly, spiritual reconciliation can refer to any process of finding peace with the divine, with the universe, or even with one's own conscience.

4. Between Conflicting Ideas or Facts (Intellectual)

Reconciliation also means making two things that seem to contradict each other fit together or coexist without contradiction.

When you reconcile two conflicting ideas, you find a way to explain how both can be true, or you resolve the apparent contradiction between them.

Example: Scientists work hard toward the reconciliation of quantum mechanics and general relativity — two theories that each work brilliantly in their own domain but seem to contradict each other at a fundamental level.

Another example: "I struggle with the reconciliation of his kind personality and the terrible things he did." — Here, the speaker is trying to make sense of two things that feel impossible to put together.

5. In Accounting and Finance (Technical)

In business and finance, reconciliation has a precise technical meaning: the process of comparing two sets of records to ensure they match, and identifying and explaining any differences between them.

Example: Bank reconciliation is when a company compares its own internal records of money coming in and going out with the bank's official statement, to make sure both show the same numbers. If they don't match, the difference must be found and explained.

This use of the word follows the same logic: two things that should agree are brought into agreement.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does mean.

  • Reconciliation is not the same as forgetting. You can reconcile with someone while still remembering what happened. In fact, genuine reconciliation usually requires remembering and honestly confronting the past.
  • Reconciliation is not the same as forgiveness alone. Forgiveness is one part of the journey, but reconciliation is the fuller restoration of the relationship or state of harmony. You can forgive someone privately in your heart without fully reconciling with them (especially if the relationship itself cannot or should not be restored, such as in cases of abuse).
  • Reconciliation is not always fully achievable. Sometimes people attempt reconciliation but only reach a partial restoration — a "co-existence" rather than a warm relationship. That can still be called reconciliation, even if it's incomplete.
  • Reconciliation is not instant. It is almost always a process, not a single moment. It takes time, effort, honesty, and often a willingness from both sides.

"Reconciliation" carries a sense of earnestness, seriousness, and depth. It's not a casual word. When you use it, you are signalling that the break that happened was significant, and that the effort to repair it is equally significant.

It often carries emotional weight — hope, relief, grief, difficulty. It acknowledges that something was genuinely broken, and that healing it matters.
How to Use the Word in Sentences

• "The reconciliation between the two companies ended years of legal disputes."
  • "She hoped for reconciliation with her estranged father before it was too late."
  • "The peace agreement was seen as the first step toward national reconciliation."
  • "His journal entries show his struggle toward reconciliation with his past mistakes."
  • "The accountant flagged the discrepancy during the monthly bank reconciliation."
  • "There can be no reconciliation of these two opposing viewpoints — they are fundamentally incompatible."

Since you're a learner, it helps to know the family of words this belongs to:

  • Reconcile (verb) — to reconcile with someone; to reconcile two accounts — the action itself.
  • Reconciled (adjective) — She was finally reconciled with her sister. — the state of having completed reconciliation.
  • Irreconcilable (adjective) — irreconcilable differences — when two things or people cannot be reconciled; the break is permanent or too deep to repair. (You've likely heard this in the context of divorce — "irreconcilable differences" means the couple's problems are beyond repair.)
  • Reconciliatory (adjective) — a reconciliatory gesture — something intended to bring about reconciliation.

Reconciliation is the process of restoring harmony, trust, or agreement between two parties — whether people, groups, ideas, or records — after a state of conflict, division, or inconsistency, with the understanding that the break was real and that the restoration requires genuine effort.
